screens.title: Shell Scripting and Automation with Cron
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how a plain text file can become a powerful automation tool on your Raspberry Pi. You'll see how to write Bash scripts that combine multiple Linux commands, how to add the shebang line so the system knows which shell to run, and how to make a script executable. We'll also cover storing values in variables, reading positional arguments passed from the command line, and using conditionals and loops so scripts can make decisions and repeat work. The second half of the chapter teaches automation: how cron schedules jobs using five time fields, practical examples like running backups at three in the morning, and the handy special strings such as at reboot or daily. Finally we'll touch on systemd timers as an alternative when you need more complex scheduling. By the end you will be able to write a small system check script, run it, and schedule it to run periodically. Think about one task you do repeatedly on your Pi now — you'll soon be able to automate it.

screens.title: What is a shell script?
screens.narratorSegment: A shell script is simply a plain text file that contains one or more Linux commands which the system can run in sequence. The idea is to capture a sequence of manual steps — like printing a message, checking the date, or collecting system information — and run them the same way each time. For example, a hello script prints a greeting and the current date using command substitution. The shebang line at the top tells the operating system which interpreter to use when the file is executed. Scripts are powerful because they let you automate repetitive tasks and combine small commands into a reliable routine. A common misconception is that scripts are only for programmers; in fact they are accessible tools for anyone who wants to simplify repetitive command-line work. As an example, write a two-line script that echoes a greeting and shows the date, make it executable, and run it to confirm output. Key takeaway: scripts make repeatable tasks reliable and shareable. What is a shell script? means a shell script is a text file of shell commands that runs like a small program to automate tasks.. In practical terms, a text file of commands you can run as a program. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A shell script is a text file of shell commands that runs like a small program to automate tasks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › What is a shell script?
Core idea
Capture commands in a file so you can run them later or repeatedly without typing.
#!/bin/bash echo "Hello, Raspberry Pi!" echo "Today is $(date)"
Why it matters
  • Automates repetitive maintenance tasks like backups and checks.
  • Makes procedures reproducible and shareable across devices.
Example
Create hello.sh, add the shebang and two echo lines, run chmod +x, then run ./hello.sh to see the greeting and date.
Common misconception
Some learners assume scripts must be long or complex. Small scripts are valuable: a two-line script that logs a date is already automation.
Key Takeaway

A script packages commands into a repeatable program you can run and schedule.

screens.title: Shebang and Making a Script Executable
screens.narratorSegment: Two small steps make a text file behave like a program. First, add the shebang line at the top of the file. This line begins with the hash symbol followed by an exclamation and identifies which shell interpreter will run the commands. On many systems you use the path to bash. The shebang ensures your script runs with the expected shell behavior for variables, expansions, and built-in commands. Second, set the execute permission so the operating system treats the file as runnable. Use the file permission command to add execute for the file owner. Then run the script using a path such as dot-slash followed by the filename to run the version in the current directory. A common error is to forget the execute bit and then wonder why invoking the file does nothing; another is to rely on a different shell by invoking the script without a shebang and getting unexpected expansion rules. Example: create a script with a shebang, run the permission change command, then run it and confirm the expected output appears. Takeaway: shebang plus execute permission makes scripts predictable and runnable.

keyIdea.title: Run-ready scripts
keyIdea.text: Shebang selects the interpreter; chmod +x gives execute permission; use ./ to run from the current directory.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Shebang & Executable
Shebang
Identifies the shell interpreter so your script runs with predictable behavior.
#!/bin/bash
echo "Hello, Raspberry Pi!"
Make executable
Run the permission command to add execute permission to your script. Then execute using the path to the file so the shell runs that script rather than searching PATH.
Example walkthrough
Create hello.sh with a shebang. Run the permission command to make it executable. Run dot-slash hello.sh and observe the greeting and date output appear.
Common mistake
Forgetting to set the execute permission is the most common reason a script won't run as expected. Also check the shebang path matches an installed interpreter on your system.
Key Takeaway

A shebang plus execute permission makes a text file run reliably as a script.

screens.title: Variables and Command Substitution
screens.narratorSegment: Variables let your script hold values for reuse so you aren't repeating literals. You assign a name an equals sign and a value without spaces around the equals sign. Then you reference that variable later to insert its value or to build dynamic messages. For example, setting a user name variable and then echoing a greeting with that variable makes your script customizable. Command substitution is how a script captures the output of a command and uses it as text; a common pattern captures the current date into a message so the script prints when it ran. A practical example: assign a name variable, then echo a message that includes the current date captured from the date command. A misunderstanding students have is expecting variables to persist across separate runs — they do not unless saved externally; each script run starts with a fresh environment unless you export or write state to a file. Takeaway: variables and command substitution make scripts flexible and informative. Variables and Command Substitution means use variables to store values and command substitution to include command output inside script text.. In practical terms, store values and embed command output inside scripts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Variables & substitution
keyIdea.text: Use variables to store values and command substitution to include command output inside script text.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Variables & Command Substitution
Storing values
Assign a value and reference it later so the script is easier to update and reuse.
USER_NAME="Alex"
echo "Hello, $USER_NAME!"
Command substitution runs a command and inserts its output where needed. Use it to include dynamic data like the current date.
Concrete example
echo "Today is $(date)" prints a line that includes the system date at the moment the script runs.
Misconception
Variables set in a script do not persist across separate runs unless you write them to a file or export them into a persistent environment.
Key Takeaway

Use variables and command substitution to make scripts adaptable and informative.

screens.title: Accepting Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: Scripts can accept information when you run them by using positional parameters. The first value provided after the script name is accessible as the first positional parameter, the second as the second, and so on. This allows a single script to perform different work based on inputs without editing the file. For instance, a script can print the first and second arguments so you can pass a user name and a mode like start or stop. A common student mistake is to assume missing arguments default to empty strings without handling that case; scripts should check whether required arguments are present and display usage instructions if not. A short pattern is to test for the presence of the first argument and show an explanatory message if absent. Example: echo the values of the first and second argument to confirm they are passed correctly during testing. Takeaway: positional parameters make scripts flexible and reusable across contexts. Accepting Arguments means use $1, $2, etc., to read command-line arguments so a single script can behave differently based on input.. In practical terms, make scripts configurable by using positional parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Accepting Arguments
Positional parameters
Pass values when you run the script so the same script can handle different inputs without editing.
echo "First argument: $1"
echo "Second argument: $2"
Example
Run the script with two words after the filename. The script will print those words so you can verify arguments are passed correctly.
Validation tip
Check for required arguments and show a usage message if they are missing. This prevents silent failures when scripts expect input.
Key Takeaway

Arguments let one script handle many cases; always validate inputs to avoid mistakes.

screens.title: Conditionals: Making Decisions in Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Conditionals allow a script to choose different actions depending on input or state. The pattern checks a condition and, if true, runs the following commands. You can chain additional tests with an else-if branch and provide a default action with else. This makes scripts more robust and user-friendly because they can respond to different modes like start or stop. A concrete example uses the first positional parameter: if it equals the word start, the script prints a starting message; if it equals stop, it prints stopping; otherwise it prints a usage hint. A frequent misconception is confusing the equality operator with assignment; in a conditional you compare values rather than setting them. Another trap is relying on unquoted parameters that may be empty or contain spaces; quoting parameters prevents syntax errors. Practice: write the conditional example, run it with different arguments, and observe the differing output. Takeaway: conditionals let scripts make choices and present clear usage when inputs are unexpected. Conditionals: Making Decisions in Scripts means use if, elif, and else to handle different inputs and guide script behavior cleanly.. In practical terms, use if, elif, and else to adapt behavior based on input. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Control flow
keyIdea.text: Use if, elif, and else to handle different inputs and guide script behavior cleanly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Conditionals
If / Elif / Else pattern
Make decisions based on input values so your script can act differently in different modes.
if [ "$1" = "start" ]; then
  echo "Starting..."
elif [ "$1" = "stop" ]; then
  echo "Stopping..."
else
  echo "Usage: script.sh start|stop"
fi
Concrete example
Run with start to see the starting message, run with stop to see the stopping message, and run with no argument to see the usage line.
Common mistake
Unquoted parameters can break the test when values are empty or contain spaces. Always quote parameters in conditionals to avoid syntax errors.
Key Takeaway

Use conditionals to make scripts responsive to input and to provide helpful usage messages.

screens.title: For Loops: Iterating a Fixed Set
screens.narratorSegment: A for loop repeats a block of commands for each item in a list or sequence. This is useful when you want to run the same check across multiple files, devices, or items. The loop sets a loop variable to each value in turn and runs the contained commands. For example, iterating numbers from one to five and printing a count demonstrates basic repetition. Another common use is looping over filenames returned by a pattern. Beware of naive patterns that break on filenames with spaces; for simple practice use explicitly listed values or ensure proper quoting. A misconception is that loops are only for complex programs — in shell scripting, simple loops often replace repetitive manual invocations. Practice: write a loop that prints a numbered line five times, then adapt it to iterate over three filenames and echo each name. Takeaway: for loops provide concise repetition for many small automation tasks. For Loops: Iterating a Fixed Set means use for loops to repeat commands over a list of items or a simple sequence.. In practical terms, repeat actions for collections of items or fixed sequences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use for loops to repeat commands over a list of items or a simple sequence.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › For Loops
Repeat with for
Loop over items or numbers to perform a repeated action without copying lines.
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  echo "Count: $i"
done
Example
Use a for loop to iterate over a short list of files or a sequence of numbers when you need repeated checks or reports.
Gotcha
When iterating filenames, be careful with names that include spaces. Quoting and safe patterns help avoid broken loops.
Key Takeaway

For loops eliminate repetitive typing by running the same commands for each item in a list.

screens.title: While Loops: Repeat Until a Condition Changes
screens.narratorSegment: A while loop repeats a set of commands as long as a given condition evaluates as true. This pattern is useful when the number of iterations isn't known ahead of time but depends on state, such as waiting for a sensor reading to reach a threshold or counting until a stop condition. A clear example initializes a counter at one and repeats until the counter exceeds five, incrementing each time. Scripts using while loops should guard against infinite loops by ensuring the condition will eventually become false. A common misconception is that loops should run forever for monitoring; instead, prefer scheduled runs or include sleep delays and explicit exit conditions to avoid high C P U use. Practice writing a while loop that counts and sleeps briefly between iterations for a safe repeated check. Takeaway: while loops provide conditional repetition but must be written with escape conditions and responsible pacing. While Loops: Repeat Until a Condition Changes means use while loops for conditional repetition; ensure they include a termination condition and sensible pacing.. In practical terms, continue looping while a condition remains true. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: While loops
keyIdea.text: Use while loops for conditional repetition; ensure they include a termination condition and sensible pacing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › While Loops
Repeat while a condition is true
Use while loops when the number of repetitions depends on changing state.
count=1
while [ $count -le 5 ]; do
  echo "Count: $count"
  count=$((count + 1))
done
Example
A loop that polls a sensor value, sleeps a short time between checks, and exits when a threshold is reached.
Common mistake
Forgetting to change the condition or add a sleep can produce an infinite loop that consumes system resources.
Key Takeaway

Ensure while loops include a clear termination condition and, when appropriate, a short sleep to pace checks.

screens.title: Automation with cron: crontab and Editing Jobs
screens.narratorSegment: Cron is a scheduler that runs commands on a repeating timetable. To add or edit jobs for your user, open the crontab editor for that user. Each cron entry specifies when the job runs using five time fields followed by the command to execute. Common practice is to call scripts from cron with absolute paths and to redirect output to a log file so you can review results later. For a daily backup at three in the morning, specify zero minutes and three hours with wildcards for the remaining fields. For frequent monitoring, specify a step field to run a job every ten minutes. A common issue is using relative paths or assuming environment variables; cron runs with a minimal environment, so use full paths and include any necessary environment setup inside the script. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › cron: crontab & Jobs
Scheduling with cron
Use crontab to add scheduled entries that run commands at specific times.
crontab -e
# Example: run backup at 03:00 daily
0 3 * * * /home/alex/backup.sh
Tip: redirect output to a log file so you can verify runs later, for example append standard output and error to a timestamped log.
Example
An hourly system check can be scheduled and its output appended to a persistent log so you can inspect system state over time.
Common pitfall
Cron provides a minimal environment. Always use absolute paths and perform any environment setup inside the script to avoid missing commands or variables.
Key Takeaway

Use crontab to schedule jobs and make scripts self-contained so they run reliably under cron's limited environment.

screens.title: Cron Time Fields Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Each cron entry begins with five time fields that determine when the command runs: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. Read left to right: the minute field accepts values from zero to fifty-nine, the hour field uses zero to twenty-three, and the remaining fields accept their natural ranges. Wildcards allow matches for every value, and step expressions let you run jobs at regular intervals like every ten minutes. There are also special strings for convenience such as at reboot, hourly, and daily that map to common schedules and avoid hand-writing the five fields. A common learner mistake is misplacing fields or miscounting them — always double-check each position. The five fields

Practical examples

screens.title: Special strings, Logging, and systemd timers
screens.narratorSegment: Special strings in cron simplify common schedules. Instead of writing five fields, you can use words like at reboot, hourly, and daily to express common timings. Always prefer absolute paths and redirect output to a log file when scheduling scripts, because cron jobs run with minimal environment settings by default. For example, append output to a log file so each run adds a timestamped entry for later inspection. The chapter also mentions systemd timers as an alternative: they provide richer dependency control and integration with systemd services when you need more than simple periodic execution. For beginner projects, cron is usually sufficient, but if you later require triggers tied to system services or more advanced logging, systemd timers are an option. A practical hands-on task ties these ideas together: write a system_check script that prints the date, disk space, C P U temperature, and memory usage; make it executable; run it manually; then schedule it hourly in cron with output appended to a log. A common pitfall is not checking the log location or failing to include full paths so the scheduled job appears to do nothing. Takeaway: use special strings for convenience, log outputs for verification, and consider systemd timers when automation needs grow.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Special strings & Logging
Special strings
Use at reboot, hourly, daily for common schedules without writing five fields.
@reboot — run once at startup
@hourly — start of every hour
@daily — once per day
Logging & Alternatives
Redirect output so you can inspect job results. For advanced scheduling and tighter integration, systemd timers are an alternative to cron.
# Append output to a log */60 * * * * /home/yourname/system_check.sh >> /home/yourname/system_check.log 2>&1
Common pitfall: forgetting to use absolute paths or failing to redirect both standard output and error can hide failures.
Key Takeaway

Special strings and logging make cron easier to use and debug; choose systemd timers when you need richer control.

In this chapter you will learn how a plain text file can become a powerful automation tool on your Raspberry Pi. You'll see how to write Bash scripts that combine multiple Linux commands, how to add the shebang line so the system knows which shell to run, and how to make a script executable. We'll also cover storing values in variables, reading positional arguments passed from the command line, and using conditionals and loops so scripts can make decisions and repeat work. The second half of the chapter teaches automation: how cron schedules jobs using five time fields, practical examples like running backups at three in the morning, and the handy special strings such as at reboot or daily. Finally we'll touch on systemd timers as an alternative when you need more complex scheduling. By the end you will be able to write a small system check script, run it, and schedule it to run periodically. Think about one task you do repeatedly on your Pi now — you'll soon be able to automate it.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to write simple Bash scripts that chain commands and embed small programs for the Raspberry Pi, use variables and positional arguments so scripts are configurable, and apply conditionals and loops to make scripts adapt and repeat work. You will also know how to make a script executable and run it from the shell, and how to schedule scripts using cron with its five time fields and useful special strings. Finally you'll understand when systemd timers can be an appropriate alternative for more complex timing needs. Each objective gives you practical, hands-on skills: creating a script, making it runnable, automating its execution, and verifying logs. These skills let you stop repeating manual steps and instead rely on reproducible automation that runs reliably on your device. Imagine setting up a system check to run each hour and write its output to a log — that practical ability is the milestone we aim for.

These objectives turn into concrete skills you can demonstrate. First, create a text file with a shebang line and a few commands, make it executable, and run it. Second, write scripts that accept positional arguments so the same script can behave differently depending on input, for example printing status for different services. Third, use an if statement and a loop to handle simple decision-making and to repeat checks over a list of files or sensors. Fourth, edit your crontab to schedule a script and confirm its output writes to a log file. Each milestone matters because it moves you from doing things manually to relying on repeatable automation that runs while you step away. As verification, run your script manually, then wait for the scheduled run and inspect the log. That full cycle demonstrates both correctness and reliable automation.

A shell script is simply a plain text file that contains one or more Linux commands which the system can run in sequence. The idea is to capture a sequence of manual steps — like printing a message, checking the date, or collecting system information — and run them the same way each time. For example, a hello script prints a greeting and the current date using command substitution. The shebang line at the top tells the operating system which interpreter to use when the file is executed. Scripts are powerful because they let you automate repetitive tasks and combine small commands into a reliable routine. A common misconception is that scripts are only for programmers; in fact they are accessible tools for anyone who wants to simplify repetitive command-line work. As an example, write a two-line script that echoes a greeting and shows the date, make it executable, and run it to confirm output. Key takeaway: scripts make repeatable tasks reliable and shareable. What is a shell script? means a shell script is a text file of shell commands that runs like a small program to automate tasks.. In practical terms, a text file of commands you can run as a program. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Two small steps make a text file behave like a program. First, add the shebang line at the top of the file. This line begins with the hash symbol followed by an exclamation and identifies which shell interpreter will run the commands. On many systems you use the path to bash. The shebang ensures your script runs with the expected shell behavior for variables, expansions, and built-in commands. Second, set the execute permission so the operating system treats the file as runnable. Use the file permission command to add execute for the file owner. Then run the script using a path such as dot-slash followed by the filename to run the version in the current directory. A common error is to forget the execute bit and then wonder why invoking the file does nothing; another is to rely on a different shell by invoking the script without a shebang and getting unexpected expansion rules. Example: create a script with a shebang, run the permission change command, then run it and confirm the expected output appears. Takeaway: shebang plus execute permission makes scripts predictable and runnable.

Variables let your script hold values for reuse so you aren't repeating literals. You assign a name an equals sign and a value without spaces around the equals sign. Then you reference that variable later to insert its value or to build dynamic messages. For example, setting a user name variable and then echoing a greeting with that variable makes your script customizable. Command substitution is how a script captures the output of a command and uses it as text; a common pattern captures the current date into a message so the script prints when it ran. A practical example: assign a name variable, then echo a message that includes the current date captured from the date command. A misunderstanding students have is expecting variables to persist across separate runs — they do not unless saved externally; each script run starts with a fresh environment unless you export or write state to a file. Takeaway: variables and command substitution make scripts flexible and informative. Variables and Command Substitution means use variables to store values and command substitution to include command output inside script text.. In practical terms, store values and embed command output inside scripts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Scripts can accept information when you run them by using positional parameters. The first value provided after the script name is accessible as the first positional parameter, the second as the second, and so on. This allows a single script to perform different work based on inputs without editing the file. For instance, a script can print the first and second arguments so you can pass a user name and a mode like start or stop. A common student mistake is to assume missing arguments default to empty strings without handling that case; scripts should check whether required arguments are present and display usage instructions if not. A short pattern is to test for the presence of the first argument and show an explanatory message if absent. Example: echo the values of the first and second argument to confirm they are passed correctly during testing. Takeaway: positional parameters make scripts flexible and reusable across contexts. Accepting Arguments means use $1, $2, etc., to read command-line arguments so a single script can behave differently based on input.. In practical terms, make scripts configurable by using positional parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Conditionals allow a script to choose different actions depending on input or state. The pattern checks a condition and, if true, runs the following commands. You can chain additional tests with an else-if branch and provide a default action with else. This makes scripts more robust and user-friendly because they can respond to different modes like start or stop. A concrete example uses the first positional parameter: if it equals the word start, the script prints a starting message; if it equals stop, it prints stopping; otherwise it prints a usage hint. A frequent misconception is confusing the equality operator with assignment; in a conditional you compare values rather than setting them. Another trap is relying on unquoted parameters that may be empty or contain spaces; quoting parameters prevents syntax errors. Practice: write the conditional example, run it with different arguments, and observe the differing output. Takeaway: conditionals let scripts make choices and present clear usage when inputs are unexpected. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A for loop repeats a block of commands for each item in a list or sequence. This is useful when you want to run the same check across multiple files, devices, or items. The loop sets a loop variable to each value in turn and runs the contained commands. For example, iterating numbers from one to five and printing a count demonstrates basic repetition.
